items.title: Network
items.help: The routes this session's programs leave by. A route is one of the host's (Settings, Network, Proxy): the system's own, direct, a proxy, a PAC script or a program, each set once on the host. With none named, the host's own route carries them.

route.title: Route
route.description: The name of a route the host has. A route the host lacks, or one that does not open, refuses the session.

hosts.title: Destinations
hosts.description: The destinations this route is for: a host name, *.name for a name and what is under it, an address, or a regular expression matched against the whole host. Empty: every destination no other route names.

routes.title: Routes
routes.description: In order: the first route with destinations that matches decides; then the route of the account the session runs on for the account's own addresses; then the route with no destinations; then the host's route.

bypass.title: Hosts that go direct
bypass.description: In the NO_PROXY form. Empty keeps what the routes choose.

pattern.title: Hosts
pattern.description: A host name (`api.example.com`), a name and everything under it (`*.example.com`), an address, or any other regular expression, matched whole and without regard to case against the destination as the program names it (a name, or an address): `.*` matches every destination, `(api|auth)[.]example[.]com` two.

identity.title: Certificate
identity.description: `system` presents what the operating system's keystores choose by the authorities the server names, as a browser would; or the thumbprint (SHA-256, in hex) of one certificate the host lists as available.

client_certificate_hosts.title: Hosts that get a client certificate
client_certificate_hosts.description: Each entry is a pattern for hosts (a host name, *.name for a name and what is under it, an address, or any regular expression matched against the whole host: .* is every host) and the certificate to present to them: system (what your keystores choose by the authorities the server names, as a browser would) or one of the certificates this computer lists. The first entry that matches a host decides. For these hosts alone the host's proxy for the session ends the program's TLS with a certificate made on demand by an authority this host process makes in memory (never written to disk; limited to exactly these hosts when every pattern is a plain host, *.name or address) that the session's programs alone are told to trust, and makes its own TLS to the host, presenting the certificate. A program that pins the certificates it trusts, or reads no CA file variable (Windows' own tools), fails for them. Empty ends no TLS.
